speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO AREAS OF HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in June of this year I outlined a nine point employment and manpower development program. Under this program provision was made for special measures of federal assistance to designated development areas. The 35 designated development areas under this program were selected on the basis of being areas characterized by continuing high levels of unemployment and slow rates of employment growth.
In addition to qualifying for tax concessions to manufacturing and processing enterprises locating in such areas, there are additional measures designed particularly to stimulate winter employment in these designated areas. These measures include the bringing forward of federal government construction projects for this winter and higher payroll incentive payments under the municipal winter works incentive program.
The aim of the special tax incentive measures and the work of the area development agency of the Department of Industry which apply to the 35 designated development areas is primarily to stimulate year round employment in areas of slow economic growth and chronic high levels of unemployment. The additional measures that were introduced to reduce the level of unemployment in these areas during the coming winter months include a supplementary federal winter construction program and the provision for an additional 10 per cent, or a total of 60 per cent, of payroll costs of municipal winter works.
The purpose of the supplementary government construction program and the higher percentage for municipal works is to help alleviate the problem of high winter unemployment. The designation of areas for purposes of the area development program was not primarily concerned with high winter unemployment, but rather with areas of long term unemployment and slow growth.
As one means of extending the impact of the supplementary federal winter construction program, areas with heavy winter unemployment have been selected to supplement the
already designated development areas. In addition, municipalities in these areas of high winter unemployment will receive 60 per cent of payroll costs under the municipal winter works incentive program, as in the case of the designated development areas. To qualify as an area of high winter unemployment, the average ratio of national employment service registrations to estimated paid workers must have been in excess of 25 per cent in the three winter months January, February and March during the years 1961, 1962 and 1963. In all there are 45 such national employment service areas which qualify as areas of high winter unemployment.
With the consent of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like to have a table of those areas printed in Hansard as part of my statement.

an aid not only for winter employment in this country but also for those areas that are underdeveloped.
In so far as the increase in the percentage of labour costs from 50 per cent to 60 per cent is concerned, this is a move in the right direction. Naturally I should like to point out that if we are going to keep the participation of the provinces and municipalities up to a level where they have a real interest in this proposition, a warning should be issued that this percentage must not go too high. The success of these programs depends on consultations with the municipalities and provinces to make sure that their legitimate interests under the constitution are protected.

In so far as the newly developed areas are concerned, this is a subject which I feel will have to be examined with great care to make certain that the criteria we should apply at all times, namely participation in the discussions and planning at all levels of government, are maintained.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO AREAS OF HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally the house is happy to hear the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) with regard to the regulations and the benefits granted to areas known as designated areas. There is one point, however, I should like to draw to the house's attention. It is that in the selection of designated areas, the criteria taken into account were not, in my opinion, the most appropriate in the circumstances.
It seems that the selection was restricted to those areas where unemployment has been prevailing in the last eight years. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that those are not necessarily the areas in greatest need, because it is quite possible that districts which have only known unemployment in the last three or four years find themselves in a more difficult situation than others where it has existed for eight years.
Mr. Speaker, there is another factor that is noteworthy. In fact, there does not seem to have been any consultation between the various governments concerned, that is the federal authorities, the provinces and the municipal councils.
Since the government seems determined to continue examination of the situation in other districts so as to give them the benefits provided in the legislation, as soon as they meet established criteria, I strongly suggest that the minister and the government should take

that step in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities concerned.
Personally, I know that several towns in the Saguenay region have been recognized while others have not been. Granted, the government cannot recognize every city and area in Canada, but I hope just the same that it will give an answer to those which have asked to be designated as distressed areas so that municipal authorities may find out directly from the minister exactly why their municipalities cannot be recognized.
Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks, I should like to tell the minister how much we appreciate the assistance given to those regions which will benefit thereby. I am glad for their sake, but I do hope that the government will find, as soon as possible, other means than the one just described to deal with unemployment, because even if the step the government intends to take is designed to help municipalities undertake a greater amount of winter work projects, it will bring about debt increases and impose a heavier burden on municipalities which, for the most part, already have to carry a heavy load and cannot afford to go more deeply into debt.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO AREAS OF HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the policy announced by the Minister of Labour will be of some value to those districts which have been selected as designated development areas. However, I point out that there are many areas in Canada which have not been so designated. I think experience will show that we will have to reduce the criteria which the department has set up. For one thing, the levels of unemployment required are much too high. Second, the data which have been collected have been based on summer employment, which is not necessarily related to what the winter unemployment situation will be. Therefore, while this will be of some help to the districts fortunately designated, it is not going to be of much assistance to many areas which will experience severe unemployment this winter.
I would have hoped that the government would consider-and I still hope they will consider-first the possibility of applying the 60 per cent generally to municipalities under the winter works incentive program; and second, that they would consider restoring the reduction in the period during which the winter works incentive program is applicable. When a few months ago the Minister of Labour, without consulting the provinces or the municipalities, reduced this period, I think he very considerably reduced the benefit of this program and its efficacy in dealing with unemployment. I think the

government would do well to examine both the question of raising the percentage for all municipalities and second, the question of the need for restoring the two months, one at the beginning and one at the end, which were taken off the operative period a few months ago.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL ASSISTANCE TO AREAS OF HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are happy to see that the government has decided to increase by 10 per cent its share of payroll costs that municipalities have to bear under the winter works program, in order to check unemployment in Canada, especially in underdeveloped areas.
However, let us not fool ourselves, that will certainly not solve all the problems because municipalities, even if they have to assume only 10 per cent of the cost, have a very hard time trying to meet their obligations everywhere in Canada. The employment problem is relatively easy to solve when municipalities have the money or credit needed to pay the workers.
But they must face another problem, the problem of mechanization, of automation and of the purchase of materials for the building of streets and sidewalks in those municipalities.
Now, the minister is aware that these municipalities have difficulties in obtaining the necessary funds. This measure will help them to some extent, but will not settle the problem, I have no doubt about that. Nevertheless, this measure means that the federal government is willing to pay 60 per cent of labour costs in all those municipalities. It is better than nothing, but not much more, and we believe that a better legislation could be brought forward that would stem unemployment once and for all in our country and in our economically weak areas.

RETIREMENT OF VETERAN MEMBER OF SECURITY STAFF
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege. I admit at once that in doing so I may not be strictly within the rules of order, but I imagine there are many hon. members who will accept what I have to say as a question of privilege.
I believe our security police in the House of Commons are famous throughout the world because they carry out their job of protection without violence, batons or guns. Today James Kealey is retiring from the security staff after having served for 28 years. When he first came to the House of Commons the security staff numbered only 16; now they are more than 70. I believe that we in this House of Commons should honour our security staff and in particular, today, one by the name of Kealey. That is why I am asking, on a question of privilege, that you, Mr. Speaker, will convey to the security staff, our thanks for their services and their courtesy, and that especially you will convey to Mr. Kealey, as one of the original staff, our thanks for the courtesy and understanding with which he

Questions
has handled the many thousands of people who have visited this building and say to him that in so doing he has conveyed an admirable public relations picture of this House of Commons.
I should like to pay tribute to Mr. Kealey on this day when he is leaving the security staff and, in so doing, convey my thanks to the entire security staff of the House of Commons.

Has any consideration been given to assisting Canadian export manufacturers in a manner similar to the A.I.D. program of the United States and, if so, what are the details?
Answer: Under section 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act long term Canadian government financing up to 25 years is available in connection with the sale abroad of Canadian capital equipment. The normal interest rate for such financing is 6 per cent. In addition, in the pure aid context, capital equipment and capital projects as well as certain commodities of Canadian origin are supplied to the underdeveloped areas under Canadian grant aid programs, in particular the Colombo plan. In these instances, of course, no repayment or interest is involved.
In contrast aid supplied to the underdeveloped areas by the United States agency for international development (AID) takes the form, in large measure, of long term low interest loans covering the supply of both capital equipment and a variety of commodities. These loans involve maturities of up to 40 years with extensive grace periods during which no repayment of principal is required. Interest rates are nominal or very low.
The essential difference in the facilities available to Canadian and U.S. exporters is that the former are in a position to take advantage of loans running to 25 years and grants to less developed countries while the latter enjoy the advantages provided by longer terms loans at low rates of interest.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the reported difficulties and delays he experienced over the week end in reaching President Kennedy, would the Prime Minister state whether any means are being taken to improve direct communications with the President, and at the same time he might tell the house the results of his talk with the President.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to the hon. gentleman for giving me the opportunity to state there were no difficulties nor delays, and that any reports to that effect were based on a complete misrepresentation of the facts of the situation.
Because of that misrepresentation and the publicity given to it perhaps I had better put on the record exactly what happened. Immediately after the debate on this matter on Friday morning, and on Friday afternoon, I instructed that the record of that debate be 28902-5-225J
Inquiries of the Ministry sent at once to our embassy in Washington for the benefit of the state department and the White House, so that when I talked with the President he would have the record before him. That was done immediately, and at the end of the afternoon I phoned our embassy in Washington and asked them to get in touch with the White House to see if the President had a chance to study that record and if the President would be available to talk to me that evening.
I got a reply immediately that the President would be very glad to talk to me at once, or at any time convenient to me. At that time he was in conference over a dangerous situation developing in access to Berlin, and his office said if I preferred to wait until that meeting was over he would speak to me afterward and he would have the benefit of reading our record. I said I wanted to give him enough time to read the record, and I called him after breakfast on Saturday morning.
Any reports that there were difficulties or delays on this matter are designed merely to stir up this kind of anti-American sniping which is most unfortunate when we already have so many difficulties with the United States.
As a supplementary question, I wonder whether the Prime Minister would answer the second part of my question and state the results of his talk.

Mr. Speaker, I had a talk of 15 to 20 minutes with the President on the telephone and acquainted him, as a supplement to what he had already read, with the feelings of the House of Commons, the government and, I thought, the feelings of the people of Canada with regard to the very serious situation that had developed because of what I considered to be, and what I stated in the house was, an unhelpful intervention by the United States secretary of labour, who himself was with the President when he spoke to me, and with regard to the more than shocking intervention of the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O.
I called the President's attention to the seriousness of the situation and expressed the hope, and more than a hope, that when the Canadian parliament took action in this matter and government trusteeship was a fact, that decision would be accepted by all concerned in the United States.

As a supplementary question may I ask the Prime Minister whether he received any assurance from the President that the government of the United States would co-operate with the trusteeship which this parliament has authorized the government to appoint,

Inquiries of the Ministry and whether we would have the United States government's co-operation in seeing that Canadian shipping in American ports would be free from harassment and sabotage?

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that the government of the United States will co-operate in this matter, as indeed the President's statement, issued on Saturday, indicated. I cannot give the same assurance with respect to United States labour unions and the leadership of some of those unions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a related question of the Prime Minister. In this telephone conversation with the President did he discuss at any time this similar situation which is happening in relation to the divulging of information by the United States department of agriculture about our secret exchange of information on wheat sales?

Mr. Speaker, I think I did quite enough at that time to make the feelings of the government and parliament known with regard to the matter I talked to him about, the situation on the great lakes. speechtext: Well, as the hon. member knows, the report has been on the table, I think for nearly a week, and has been printed in Votes and Proceedings in both languages. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my purpose today during this second supply motion of the present parliament to put in a word or two on behalf of
100,000	Canadian families who exist at what can only be described as a slum level. My intention is to describe what the situation is and then, in a positive, constructive way, to indicate the general direction in which we should move to help these people in their plight.
I therefore move, seconded by my hon. friend from Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent):
That all the words after "that" he deleted and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets the failure of the government to take effective action in regard to eastern agriculture and in particular with respect to feed grain for eastern Canada and for British Columbia so as to provide:
1.	Stability of Canadian supply and price.
2.	Opportunity for expansion of eastern production of feed grain.
I think the question period today indicated to the country just where this government sits in relation to the importance of agriculture in the national scheme of things. Since this administration took office on April 22 it has given away a bit of our sovereignty in connection with the defence of our country; it has allowed our sovereignty to be attacked in fiscal policy as well as, more recently, in labour policy; and, in the last two weeks, even in agriculture. Yet when I asked the Prime Minister if he had been in touch with the President on Saturday and raised this important matter of the attacks made on us in respect of the agreement between ourselves and the United States with regard to wheat sales, he said in effect that he was occupied with more important things than the subject of agriculture.
This is not an isolated case. The hon. member for Lake St. John asked the right hon.

gentleman when he intended to bring in the bill concerning the two ministers of agriculture, and his answer was that this would be done when the house had got through other, more important business, or words to that effect. This attitude overlooks the fact that 100,000 farm families in Canada, mostly in eastern Ontario and Quebec and the mari-times, are living at levels which, if they existed in our big cities such as Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto or Montreal, would be considered as slums. If these slums existed in our big cities the entire resources of our nation, federal, provincial and municipal as well as private, would be brought to bear so as to eliminate or improve them.
We must face the fact here in Canada that this house, as presently constituted, and the people who report the news from this house do not really care about these 100,000 families. All one has to do is take a look at the press gallery at the present moment. All one has to do is take a look at the government side-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: Take a look at your own side.

maintopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext:
If we do this we will realize that neither by legislation nor by administrative action is this government doing anything to tell the story of these people or improve their conditions.
My remarks today will be along the theme that any party which hopes to remain the government of this country or to become the government of this country must realize that there is more than just one group of people in the country. Five or six years ago our national strength was being weakened. Because the maritimes were falling behind the national level of living, because the prairies had fallen behind the national level of living, as a result the government changed in 1957.
Now we come to the situation in 1963, with the old government returned and having no apparent awareness that there are anomalies in the living conditions of the Canadian people. I intend to show, Mr. Speaker, that this knowledge is available to the government and they are not doing a thing about it.
First of all, this country cannot remain strong if some segments of the economy or some areas are weakened. As I said a moment ago, that was demonstrated in the 1957 and 1958 campaigns when whole sections of the country which were not traditionally Conservative changed and elected a Conservative government. The same situation is with us today. We made certain efforts to improve the situation, but those efforts are now being abandoned. This country cannot maintain and build up its present position if agriculture
Eastern Agricultural Policy hacking goes back to the conditions that existed before 1957.
On the subject of national unity there is a great deal of talk about our cultural and language relationships. This is all good and fine, but we cannot overlook economic relationships. I wish to say very bluntly that unless we realize the structural unity of Canada as a whole, both geographically and by occupation, there cannot be strength in our economy. For example, during the last four years we sold western grain in export markets, and this immediately took the pressure off the livestock and poultry industries. Prices rose to a point where eastern farmers could come in and take up the production that was abandoned by western farmers. As a result farm income in all sections of country has risen in the last three or four years, but not equally.
I intend to put on the record farm income figures to show just what the situation has been in Canada over the last 10 years. I begin with the year 1954 for three very good reasons. This was the end of the construction period in Europe and Asia after the war. This was the end of the Korean war. This was the beginning of competitive markets for agriculture all over the world. I am also going to use realized net income figures, and the reason is simple. Realized net income is what is left after the farmer has subtracted from his gross income his cost of production and depreciation on his buildings and machinery. The result is what is left the farmers' pocket, and that is called realized net income. I am not going to use net income figures because they are purely statistical figures of use only to bookkeepers and accountants and those who keep statistics. They are completely meaningless from the point of view of showing the situation of the farmer. At this time I should like to ask permission of the house to place on Hansard the realized net income figures per farm by regions from 1954 to 1962.

This year it is going ahead at the rate of about 6 per cent. That gives an average across the country of about $2,700 in the last five years, or an increase in the national average from $2,000 in the period 1954 to 1957 to $2,700 in the period 1958 to 1962.
But when you examine the figures for regions you get an altogether different story. Listen to these figures for the maritime region: 1954, $929; 1955, $884; 1956, $1,040; 1957, $1,027; 1958, $1,138; 1959, $1,134; 1960, $1,411. In 1961 the figure dropped to $1,107 and in 1962 it continued downward to $980.
This is my point. If there are any maritime members in the house at the moment I am sure they will agree this indicates that a definite regional policy should be evolved and put forward in the house to help the people in the maritimes meet the problem of declining income.

In the period from 1958 to 1962 the figure moved up to around $1,800 and in one year went as high as $1,900, but the figure is not moving

Canada.
Ontario is slightly below the average. The figure rose from $2,100 in 1954 to $2,570 in 1962, a gain of approximately $400 per year per farm during that 10 year period.
Years ago the farmers of the prairie region used to have realized net incomes of approximately $3,400 or $3,500. By 1955 that figure had declined to $1,831 per farm. This means that in 1955 realized net income per farm on the prairies was roughly half what it had been a few years before. This is one reason why there was a big change in political allegiance there. With another government in power subsequent to that time farm income on the prairies increased steadily until 1962, when the average was $3,900 per farm or almost double in a period of six or seven years.
In British Columbia the figure in 1954 was $2,033 per farm and by last year it had climbed to $3,400. This is a very nice increase, but in summary my point is this. If you look at the realized net income figures per farm across Canada you will see that the national average is going up. There is a steady growth in British Columbia, and the farmers of the prairie provinces have almost doubled their income in that period. Ontario has had a steady growth, though a little slower than it should be. Quebec has barely increased above a static level. There has been a very small increase per year. In the maritimes, however, the figure has been declining.
I give these figures as a starting point to show how in working out policies you have to look at the income by regions. The prairies were away down in 1955 and 1956 but have now risen to their highest level. So we have an up and down type of income picture. But

you cannot take income figures as the sole criterion. What you have to do is examine the amount of investment, and on this score the eastern farmers are being treated unjustly from the point of view of income. Even on this score there is injustice being carried on so far as the income of eastern farmers is concerned.

In the maritimes in 1958 the farm family income per farm from sources other than farming-to which you should add the other figure I have quoted-was $1,461. If you recall the figures which I gave previously you will realize this means that the average for the maritimes is roughly $1,000 a year realized net income from farming, and you have to add to that this figure of $1,461. In other words more than half the income of the maritime farmers came from off-farm employment. One cannot live on $1,000 a year and therefore the whole family has to go out and do other work.
In Quebec the figure for off-farm income per family was $1,356 in 1958, and you have to add to that the figure which I quoted for Quebec for 1962 which was $1,880, to get the total income.
In Ontario the average farm family income from off-farm sources was $1,733, and if you add that to the Ontario figure which I gave earlier, you get the very substantial sum of $4,200 or $4,300.
The prairies, of course, do not have these opportunities and the average income per farm from off-farm sources was only $888. In British Columbia, however, this income was exceptional. Apparently they have very good opportunities and the average there was $2,155. The average for Canada as a whole was $1,302 per farm per year.

I put this table on the record, not to emphasize it but to show that if a government is going to draw policy out of these figures it has to know there is a great variation in income. If you put all these three tables together, region by region, it is very clear that the problem areas of Canada are eastern Ontario, Quebec, and the maritime provinces, and it is not right that these people should be doomed to continuing declining income because a government fails to realize that these people are Canadians and need equal treatment with farmers in other parts of Canada.

maintopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: I think we all realize these figures. In fact we have known of those figures since 1958 to 1963, and I am just wondering what the hon. gentleman and his government did during that time to raise those figures, and if he has any ideas how to do it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that very
question illustrates my point in such vivid terms that it makes the rest of my speech almost meaningless. Here we have a member of parliament who has been elected by a constituency, who holds forth in his constituency as a man worthy of sitting in this house, and he does not even know what the previous government did over six years. He does not even know that for the first time in Canadian history the government of the day stood up and announced on August 30, 1958, a national agricultural policy for Canada. He does not even know what the points in that agricultural policy are.

maintopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext: We know the results.

maintopic: FEED GRAIN FOR EASTERN CANADA AND B.C.
speechtext:
Yes, we know the results too. Across Canada, in the farm areas where they read the farm papers, the people showed the results in June, 1982 and April of 1963. They showed where they stood in every province.
I am going to list the points in the national farm policy announced by the then prime minister on August 30, 1958. First there was a policy of accelerated sales, and if any person has not heard about accelerated sales of farm products in the last few months he must be dead and buried. Then as No. 2 there was a flexible support policy to stabilize prices; No. 3, crop insurance to stabilize income; No. 4, a modern system of farm credit; No. 5, a multiple resources use policy; No. 6, an agricultural rehabilitation and development act, which is the ARDA program, and the 7th was a regional program for areas not benefiting completely from the national program.
It is my point here that when we introduced the acreage payments in 1958, that was a regional policy to help western Canada, because at that time farmers there had a very low level of income. In fact farm incomes were just about half what they were a few years before. The other provinces do not go up and down in income as drastically as we do in western Canada. That regional policy was put into effect where it was most needed, and it has shown results. I am suggesting that the income figures I have given show that there has to be a regional policy to help those areas of Canada which need help. I refer to eastern Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, because the income figures of those areas show trouble.
This is the motion before the house, that we regret the government has not done anything about this problem. We say this house regrets the failure of the government to take effective action in regard to eastern agriculture. This is what the motion of condemnation covers.
What happened? In 1962, as the minister responsible for agriculture I made speeches in this house and all across the country in every province saying that western farm income was beginning to rise and that we had the green light ahead in our sales of grain for export. I said this would bring a rise in livestock prices all across Canada. Therefore I asked the support of western farmers in 1962; I asked them to support my concentrating my attention as minister on the problems of eastern agriculture.

My ministers recognize that livestock is occupying a position of increasing importance in Canadian agriculture. That was the clearcut declaration of our intention in the speech from the throne in September, 1962. In October, 1962, to show that we realized what was the basic cause of the trouble, we held here in Ottawa the national conference on agricultural education to back up the multi-million dollar program we had in vocational training. We brought in representatives of all the provinces, their agricultural ministers and educational people, to see whether we could not in a co-operative fashion work out an educational program in these rural areas which would get at the basic weaknesses of these low income areas. As I say, this was done in October, 1962, and the hon. member opposite has asked, what did we do. He was much too busy going up and down this country preaching fraud, saying that the country was going downhill economically, when it was not; saying that the pegging of the dollar at 92J cents would ruin the country and force prices up, when it would not; saying that we had lost the confidence of our friends the Americans. speechtext: They know that their great strongholds of Quebec and Saskatchewan are now slipping. In fact I think they have slipped already in Saskatchewan. Let me tell you what else they did. I can tell from the reaction, Mr. Speaker, that my speech is striking home. What does this government do? They knew the facts about the situation in eastern Canada as well as we did; they knew the facts of what I call the very depressed areas. In 1963 we went out and campaigned to be given a chance to put this policy into effect. In 1957 and 1958 we campaigned on a national program for agriculture. We did put it into effect and it helped agriculture. The farmers were grateful, as their votes showed. But we could not be complacent with this program when three quarters of the farmers were doing all right and the other quarter were going downhill. That is why in 1963 we thought the policy about which I have been speaking should be implemented. What did the Liberal party do in 1963? They went into western Canada and told the western farmer, "Do not bother with this man's policy to help eastern Canada; go for $2 per bushel of wheat and $1 for the first 300 bushels for domestic wheat products." They held this out like a great big bribe. What

have they done to date? They sit there silent because they know this is one of the tangible lies that was told.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to come now to the conclusion to be drawn from this report. Figures are meaningless unless you put them into human relationship, and I am going to try to put these figures into human relationship. I refer to the table covering the 660 farms surveyed last January. Referring to the group receiving $2,500 or under for sales of farm products, we find that 43 per cent of the families in these five provinces had a total income per farm, which includes off-farm income from all members of the family, of $2,800 or less. If I may repeat, 43 per cent of the farmers in Quebec, the maritimes and eastern Ontario have an income of $2,800 including all the income from the school teacher, the husband driving the bus, the children cutting trees in the bush, maple syrup and everything else. When you think of the average number of children involved, this means, in effect, that 10, 12 or 13 Canadians are trying to live on a total income of $2,800 or less on each of these farms.
I maintain that there is a slum condition here. I maintain that the government has not tackled the problem or shown any sign of tackling the problem. Of the 43 per cent of farmers surveyed, whose main interest is farming, according to their own statements, and 53 per cent of their income comes from the farm and 33 per cent from off-farm sources, and 14 per cent from social payments. These are the people about whom I am talking. These conditions exist all across Canada but most important, so far as members are concerned, in eastern Ontario, the clay belt and in Quebec and the maritimes.
Now, I have laboured here in the hope that by putting these figures on the record I could get the house in a mood to consider possible courses of action. If you look at those people not on the commercial farms and try to visualize a farmer making $600 or $700 a year cash off the farm, he has anything from five to ten youngsters ranging in ages from five to six years up to 40 years of age. They are on the farm, and if they leave and go to the cities they will be unemployed. So they do not dare leave the farm, because when they are at home they at least eat. The common joke in certain parts of New Brunswick when I was down there was that "N.B." means "no breakfast" instead of "New Brunswick".
I have seen these farms and been on them. Mr. Speaker, you cannot help them by the ordinary price support legislation, by farm credit or crop insurance, or by selling things abroad, because they have very little to sell. Their fundamental problem is twofold. First

of all, they lack an educational base. By "education" I do not mean the formal education of learning to read and write and to add and subtract; I am talking simply about a knowledge of agriculture. Many farmers all across Canada in this category have no knowledge, for example, of what a few dollars worth of fertilizer will do with an acre of land. If you want some figures, in one of these provinces where you now have five to six acres to handle one animal for grazing you can handle over one animal per acre by using fertilizer. Or, to put it another way, $15 worth of fertilizer on an acre of land in a worn-out pasture in eastern Canada will produce $90 to $100 worth more beef. This is the type of legislation about which I am talking. They have never heard of these fertilizers and they certainly do not know of any program by either the federal or provincial governments designed to help them. I can give other examples of the most abysmal ignorance of these farmers concerning the assistance available to them now.
This is not a matter, Mr. Speaker, of being either Conservative or Liberal.

Well, I was hoping to finish this one part. It is not a question of being Conservative or Liberal at all. This is a question of these facts being available to the government. They were available to us and we started to move on them. They are now available to this government, but it has done nothing tangible about it. This question of education is the number one difficulty. You can talk to the premiers of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland or Ontario and they will be understanding about these things. But this is a problem which has to be faced by all Canadians, because there are over 100,000 farm families in Canada living under conditions which are a national disgrace.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, education is the first matter. The second is sociological. If the minister looks at these reports he will find, apart from lack of education and lack of training after they finish school, that these people have one thing in common, whether they live in Ontario, Quebec or the maritimes. They fear banks. They fear government credit. They fear credit, period. There is a sociological problem here which has to be met, and we have to bring some sociological attention to these problems to find out the techniques required. We can get many of these farmers to realize that if the government have done certain things for them it is not a sin to use those things which the

government have done for them. These things have to be done to implement educational and sociological programs, and we cannot wait five years.
This condition has been gradually accumulating year after year. I think I made it known probably in the fall of 1961. I tried all through the summer of 1962 to get programs worked out. I finally got a program worked out which I called the eastern feed grain and assistance bill, but although it was introduced in the house we never had time to proceed with it. I am not going to say anything more about it, but I should like to ask what this government has done. This government is going to put in two ministers of agriculture. I do not intend to say anything about that, but I do intend to read to the house what was put out as a press statement on August 22, 1963, by the present government, entitled "Feed grain policy". It says:
Mr. Hays stated that the government will request authority of parliament for a broadened feed grain policy to replace the present policy of freight assistance on western feed grains.
This is the third week we have been back in the house, Mr. Speaker, and there is no sign of anything like that appearing on the order paper.
Second:
The new policy will provide for the payment of accrued storage charges on western feed grain in licensed eastern elevators during the period October 15 to April 15.
Today is October 14, and so far nothing has appeared. Their 60 days of decision so frightened the government that they are paralyzed with fear. They now have one more day in which to move, but there is nothing on the order paper.
Third:
-the Canadian wheat board has decided to institute at once a provisional pricing system for oats and barley moved from the lakehead to eastern elevators.
Without going into the details of what a provisional pricing policy is, I pointed out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) a week ago last Friday that the provisional pricing policy was not working, and for two good reasons. One was that with this tremendous export demand there is no incentive to move that grain eastwards because the rates for moving it eastwards are better for export purposes than those rates applying to movements of grain for Canadian consumption. Second, the storage rates are better if you store grain for export rather than for domestic use. In spite of that I have not heard of any meeting yet with the board of grain commissioners to discuss this vital fact,
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking and all this information is available. This is the type of thing which was before me last spring.
Now, what about this eastern market? According to this press release, projections of future requirements indicate that 120 million bushels will be required by 1970, and 150 million by 1975. The present average use is about 85 million bushels of western feed grains. We have the largest market in the world for western feed grain in British Columbia and eastern Canada. This figure of 85 million bushels is a rough figure. In 1970, which is only six years away, it will go up to 120 million, and in 1975, which is only about 12 years away, it will go up to 150 million. And those figures are conservative figures, Mr. Speaker. Here we have a possible market of 150 million bushels. What other country in the world takes as much in an average year? And this is a steady market. The action of the government in announcing their intention on August 22 of doing something but doing nothing is reason for all members of all parties in the opposition to stand together and vote no confidence in this government.
Just to show, Mr. Speaker, the practical results of not putting this policy into effect, a week ago Friday I read a wire to the house received from the head of the maritime co-op, Mr. W. D. Dernier. I should like to read the first sentence again.
Following protest sent government on behalf domestic feeders "vigorously protest discrimination by Canadian wheat board not allowing domestic market to purchase any feeding grades wheat except immediate use. Now price advanced five and one eighth cents since Monday representing along with increase in water freight rates hundreds of thousands of dollars extra cost to domestic feeders. Captive domestic market treated unfairly in relation to export sales. If CWB uncertain over available grades for feed some provision for purchase at price levels prevailing early September should have been made.
That wire is a cry for help from the maritimes, the most sorely hit area in Canada. If you look at the costs of eastern agriculture you will find that 25 per cent of all the money spent by eastern farmers is spent on the purchase of feed grain. What we must do is to reduce these costs and increase the farmer's realized net income.
What have this government done about that? They issued a statement saying that they were going to do three things. Two of these things have not been done, as far as we have heard in this house or in the public press. This government stands petrified before the prospect of doing anything. This cry for help from the maritimes can be heard from every feeding area in Quebec. Where do the members of the Social Credit party stand on this issue? Do they intend to stand

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking up and help keep this government in power- a government which allows the prices of feed grain to rise, though they know the Conservative government, when in power, had a policy to deal with this situation? The present government says it will pay storage charges at the elevators if the brokers will take it there. But no one is taking it down, and the prices are rising. The Chinese can go into the offices of the Canadian wheat board in Winnipeg and buy grain for six months for a single price. They can have a stabilized price. The Russians bought over 200 million bushels of wheat and wheat flour at a fixed price for ten and a half months. The Japanese bought wheat for eight months at a fixed price. Even the British bought wheat at a fixed price.
But who is helping the eastern feeders to get grain at a fixed price? Certain hon. members will have the chance to show their constituents tomorrow whether they want these prices to go up and down, or whether they want a stabilized price, such as we were prepared to introduce and in respect of which we had a measure on the order paper last February.
I said also, in the course of the campaign in western Canada, that eastern farmers needed something comparable to the wheat board to look after their interests. Who is looking after the interests of the eastern feeders? Certainly, it is not the brokers in Montreal. Certainly, it is not this government. But the hon. members most affected by this problem must decide for themselves. I turn, for example, to the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard). He comes from a promising agricultural area which could achieve a tremendous increased income if a co-ordinated program for livestock and poultry rearing were introduced there. But there are certain things which must be available as a prerequisite, and among them is a supply of feed grain at a stable price, at a cost which would put the area on terms of competitive equality with the other feeding areas. We had pledged ourselves to achieve this result. I ask hon. members this: is the statement of intention which has been made on the part of this government likely to help the eastern provinces in developing along the lines I have indicated? I suggest it will do the reverse. The policy announced by the present government has done nothing to meet the situation. We suggested that the government should step in and set up an organization to look after the interests of the eastern farmers, in short to do the same for the eastern farmers as the Canadian wheat board does for the farmers of the west. We intended to use the services of a government board in co-operation with private enterprise so as to produce a

system which would result in a stable price for grain, a price which would not vary whether one lived in Bruce county, Lake St. John or Sydney. This was our policy. It is still our policy. While hon. gentlemen opposite have been talking, the price has been going up. It has gone up five cents already, and it will go up a lot more. Wait until the ice comes, and hon. members will see what happens to the price.
I have tried to set before this house something of the background of the great need among many of the farmers of eastern Canada-not all these farmers, but the 25 per cent who are in a very degraded position, the 25 per cent whose income from the farm is less than $1,200 or whose income from all sources is less than $2,800. Let us remember that in Quebec and the maritime provinces 43 per cent of the farmers live under these conditions. When we were in power we were grappling with this problem but we were thrown out of office by the big city vote. Now I ask these representatives of the big city voters to consider these people of whom I have been speaking as Canadians-to get off dead centre, to get the ship under way and do something for them.
I wish to conclude by saying that the series of statements I have made about eastern feed grain applies to many other segments of agriculture in eastern Canada. The dairy industry is a subject in itself. The dairy industry is a basic branch of agriculture. This is not a platitude. It is the background of integrated agriculture in Canada. That industry is not in serious trouble as yet, but it is heading that way. Not only does the solution require co-operation between the federal government and the provincial governments, particularly those of Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes, but it requires international co-operation as well. One of my colleagues will be speaking later on the dairy industry. I should like to leave with the minister the thought that the difficulties of that industry might be solved by getting Ontario and Quebec to agree with the federal government on a joint program, after an intensive study of the situation in Europe and the United States, two areas where there have been long-standing surpluses of dairy products. I think there is a type of cooperation which, if it were followed, might produce a solution to our difficulties.
I made a speech on this subject a few weeks ago in which I put forward a series of suggestions as to how this might be done by co-operation between Canada and the United States. I could, of course, go on to deal with this subject at great length but I think I have said enough to convince all

hon. members that a problem does exist and that, regardless of party, an attack must be made on the causes of the present situation. We cannot merely sit back and say that, on the average, farm income is rising. The figure for average income does not give a true picture of what is happening in these areas of eastern Canada. It is true that income is going up very well in some parts of Canada, but I think all hon. members should cooperate during this session of parliament to make sure that any policies which are brought forward are concentrated on the vital problems of eastern agriculture.

The hon. member has been right across Canada talking, yelling and hollering about the condition of agriculture. I have travelled in something like 32 different countries in the world and I feel that I know a little bit about agriculture. Until three years ago I owned and supervised a farm where 125 cows were milked, and I would challenge the former minister to come out to the central experimental farm with me because he cannot even milk a cow. Nor would he know how deep to put in a drill to sow an acre of wheat. Nor would he be able to plow a straight furrow.
It takes a little more, Mr. Speaker, than just looking at statistics. Statistics are for the losers. You can pump them in here, there and everywhere and I do not think they mean very much if things are pretty good. I believe that in the last six months we have done a great deal more for agriculture than has been done for many years, by the improvement of some of our old programs such as feed grain assistance, which was started in the year 1941, and many other programs that were Liberal policies to begin with, but have had their names changed.
I want to refer to an article in the London Free Press of September 28, 1963, a newspaper that has not always been on our side. It has this to say with regard to farm cash income:
Farmers' cash income from farming operations reached a record $1,449,700,000 in the first half of 1963, the dominion bureau of statistics estimated today. It was 5.8 per cent above the figure for the first half of 1962.
The estimate includes income for the cash sale of crops, Canadian wheat board participation payments on the previous year's grain crop, net cash 28902-5-226
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking advances on farm stored grains in western Canada and deficiency payments. No allowance was made for production costs incurred by farmers. Biggest factors in the increase were higher sales of wheat, coarse grains, potatoes, poultry products and cattle.
Increases in cash income were reported in all provinces except Alberta where cash receipts were 1 per cent below the 1962 first half. The Ontario total was $476,431,000, compared with $448,920,000 last year.
With respect to feed grains, we have a feed grain policy which I think will be most acceptable to the eastern farmers. I might say that not long after I was made Minister of Agriculture I attended a meeting with all the ministers of agriculture in Canada. We discussed many of the problems that were plaguing various provinces and Canada as a whole, so far as agriculture was concerned. I agree with the previous speaker that possibly Quebec has a problem. I spent two and a half days with the minister of agriculture of Quebec. We sat down with his officials and our officials and discussed many of their problems. He was quite familiar with the feed grain policy which we proposed and which we hope we can get through parliament soon. He thought it was an excellent program and that it would do a great deal to help them.
I might say that this program will pay grain storage costs. It will also put grain in location. I am happy to report to the house now that we have more grain in stock for eastern feed people than there was last year. I might read some of the figures so that the house will be familiar with the situation. These are figures as to grain stocks in various positions as at the end of September this year and last year. At Fort William-Port Arthur we had last year 5.9 million bushels of oats in stock and we have 13.5 million this year. In barley we had 5.7 million last year and this year we have 10.5 million. In eastern terminal elevators oat stocks were 17 million bushels last year and this year they are 37 million. Barley stocks last year were 19 million and this year they are 38 million.
So you can see we are sitting on top of this problem. We knew we were going to have this problem when the wheat board was able to sell such a big amount of wheat to Russia. We realized we would have to keep these grains on spot. I might also advise that last year feed grains were 81 million bushels and this year they will be up 10 per cent, so this is another increase.
We are taking a good look at the problems of the eastern farmers. You will be interested to know that right across Canada the price of milk is higher than it was a year ago and that the price of cheese is higher than it was a year ago. I want to say a word about the price of cattle. Starting in June of this year our own consumption of beef was 16 per

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking cent higher in the two top grades than it had ever been in Canada's history. This increase must have been caused by a very buoyant economy and full employment. Whenever we had 18,000 head of reds and blues in Canada in previous years we went into the export market. Since June 16 we have been consuming almost 22,000 head of reds and blues per week and we have not gone into the export market yet. The hon. member said something about acreage payments. I know there were three acreage payments made and they were $200 a farm. A fat lot of good that is to a farmer in western Canada who has a $50,000 investment. In looking at the matter I can see no sound reason for giving this amount of money, having regard to the amount of good it would do the farmer. The thing that the farmers of the west want is empty bins. We were happy and pleased when we were able to sell wheat to China and we were also happy and pleased when we were able to sell wheat to Russia.
I have farmed in eastern Canada and I have farmed in western Canada, and I know what the problems of the western farmer are. I have lain awake at night wondering how certain problems could be resolved. The most important problem facing farmers today is the high capital cost of machinery. This is the thing that needs to be examined more than any other facet of agriculture. In order to devise something, we are going to need everybody's help. I have discussed the matter with the farmers union and the federation of agriculture. I have discussed it with all the provincial ministers of agriculture. I have discussed it with seven ministers of agriculture in Europe, and said that it seemed to me this was one of the problems we must resolve.
If we are going to have the family farm we must have some sort of rental deal whereby the farmer will be able to rent the machinery he needs when he has good crops. This is the most important thing so far as the farmer is concerned. The cost of machinery is what is killing the family farm. The family farm is a most important way of life and it is most important to the consumers of Canada. You only have to go to Russia and see their system and the terrific problems they are having with production, and you will realize that the family farm is number one in importance.
The second most important thing that the farmers need in Canada today is proper facilities, to be able to finance their farms


in order to convert them into proper economic units. The Farm Credit Corporation is very good, but it does not go far enough and the lid should be taken right off. How can you tie down the farmers in western Canada or eastern Canada to $20,000 or $27,000 today when they need $25,000 or $40,000? When I was in Holland they were selling land in the polders to the farmers because they think it will give them the pride of ownership and will help the production of grain and so on. The government of Holland is doing it on a 60 year basis at an interest rate of around 3 per cent so that the land can be handed from one generation to the next. This is one of our big problems.
Our third big problem is crop disasters and taking care of the farmers when they are hailed out, dried out, blown out or frozen out. This is most important, and these are three programs which we must examine carefully. To say that the dairy farmer is not in trouble is not correct. He is in more trouble than any other type of farmer and it will require all our efforts to solve his problem.
In 1958 the previous government raised the price of butter from 58 cents to 64 cents per pound, and now we are subsidizing it at both ends, 12 cents to the consumer and a great deal to the producer. We cannot live with that sort of thing and we must think of some different way to help the dairy farmer.
Our agricultural policy has been put together, spot by spot, ever since 1935. If things went wrong in the maritimes we dumped some money over there, and that was the pattern all across the country. We have to take a long look at our agricultural policy from the Pacific coast to the Atlantic coast.
The previous speaker quoted a lot of statistics but they do not give the true story. The dairy farmer needs help and we must give it to him. The sooner we do it the better, but how can we do it when we waste so much time in this house? The first thing we should do is take a long look at the operation of the dominion government and the way we operate in this house. I have never seen such a waste of time. It is just fantastic. These are the first things we ought to be examining.

Mr. Speaker, if I might depart from the topic which has been under discussion, I would like to remind the house that today is Thanksgiving day. We all have very much to be thankful for in this great nation, even though we cannot always be thankful for the words spoken in this house. It is well we pause to recognize the fact that we have much to be thankful for in Canada.

When I picked up the Montreal Gazette this morning I was much impressed with the leading editorial, and I would like the privilege of putting part of it on the record. It
says:
At this time of the year-the season of Thanksgiving-many another country of the world used to look towards Canada as a land blessed beyond other lands.
But it is not so that the world today looks upon Canada. People in other nations are wondering what has happened to Canada, what has gone wrong. It has become a country whose hesitations have fragmented its own parliament. It is a country, despite its prosperity, that keeps questioning its future. It is a country full of quarrels and harshness, frantic boasts and foolish words, a country that struggles and sighs, and wonders and doubts.
What, then, has gone wrong, that a country with so much to be thankful for has none the less taken away the picture of strength and good fortune that it once had abroad, and has replaced it by one of dissatisfaction and fret?
Further along in the editorial it says:
The trouble with Canada today is that it may be slipping into the morbid determination to make the worst of all things; and, having made the worst, to look with dark calm upon the most desperate eventualities. What may be fading away is the constructive spirit, the will to build, the desire to save.
These are good words for us to think of here today.
Never has there been reason for any man to suspend Thanksgiving because the times were hard. Rather, he thanked God, took his courage in both hands, and went forward in faith. True thanksgiving has always been the offering of thanks for the hard task that demanded the best that any man had to give. The pioneer, for all his toil and trouble, was a thankful man.
But this may be the heritage that is in danger: the tradition of giving thanks and taking courage. Because we falter in the courage, we fumble in the thanksgiving.
And so the extreme words beget the extreme response. Doubt finds its echo in an answering doubt. Hardness of heart turns other hearts as hard. The narrow view contracts the corresponding vision. The danger is that we may be making a community of doubt, pooling our hesitations, sharing our want of faith.
On such a day as this the giving of thanks searches out the heart of a country and tests its quality. For true thansksgiving can never be a passive thing. It is not the utterance of a static mind. It is the living worship of God by those who are moving forward, with faith and vision, to the way ahead, hoping for better things.
Out of fullness of vision, courtesy of words, and with the wise admission that even faults have two sides, they are resolved to build and not to destroy, to seek and not to give up the search, to hear and not to close the mind.
Nothing in such a country could be so foolish as despair. No people have had greater opportunities laid out before them. This is as near as any land in history to being the Promised Land, a land to which the old biblical words would apply:
"For the Lord thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of the valleys and hills; a land of wheat and barley... a land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not 28902-5-226J
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass."
In such a land, and with such a people, the way must be found to share more fully the great endowment. And the way must be found to share also the inner enrichment that comes through understanding. We have every need and reason to be thankful, for an unhesitating thanksgiving would release creative faith, and make the future worthy of the present.

speechtext:
I identified it at the outset. It is today's leading editorial in the Montreal Gazette.
Mr. Speaker, having listened this afternoon to the speech of the former minister of agriculture, and thinking back over the years that have elapsed since 1957-58, we find a strange paradox in our midst. Here is a man condemning a government that has been in office approximately six months for conditions which relate to, as he said, 100,000 families in eastern Canada, in conditions that certainly are not those in which Canadians should be living today. This man is placing the blame upon the new government when actually he, and the government of which he was a member, should have done something about those conditions in the years they were in office.
I do not say that in support of the Liberal government, but the fact remains that the conditions he describes so aptly and ably exist because agricultural policies during the last four or five years were totally inadequate to meet the needs of the eastern farmers. To stand up as he has done today, and try to convince the house that it should throw out this government because of his own failure of action, is something that is just a little bit beyond understanding. Eastern farmers, particularly those in Quebec and the maritimes, would never have turned their backs on the previous government had they been satisfied that its policies were adequate to meet their needs.

Then Canada would be fulfilling the role that Canada can play, that of helping to defeat the greatest enemy we have in the world, hunger. Hunger should not exist in the world with today's potential for abundance, when we can produce enough for all the people of the world to have a basic standard of living as it relates to food, yes, and shelter and clothing as well.
This is the challenge that is before us. This is the responsibility that rests on the government. I agree that six months is not sufficient time in which to introduce all these changes. I am discouraged when I see before us in the house another attempt at political manoeuvring. Mr. Speaker, we have waited for some time for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) to make a speech in this house, and I find it unfortunate that he should make a speech in reply to an amendment moved on this occasion to grant supply. I find it unfortunate because of the fact that we had expected the present minister to outline new policies giving new hope to farmers in all parts of Canada, rather than give the tirade he did. The Minister of Agriculture said during his statement that he would like to challenge someone to milk cows, and I hereby challenge him. I think arrangements could be made at the experimental farm, and anybody who fills a 12-quart pail selected by officials at the farm in the shortest time would be winner. I would be happy to accommodate the minister, even though I have not done any agricultural activity for a long time. I would also be quite happy to help plow some of the fields, if that could be considered too. This may have been an idle challenge, Mr. Speaker, and if it was then I am unhappy about it. If it is not an idle challenge it may produce some interest in agriculture in Ottawa, and allow people to see the experimental farm. If it brought about that result I think it would have accomplished something for some members of parliament.
It is unfortunate that the amendment moved today has been worded in the way it has, for the simple reason that it has produced recriminations, as well as a great deal of harsh language in a political sense, between the two parties. We have heard talk about things the official opposition would have done had they been in office, and because they were not they were not done. The Canadian public, and particularly the agricultural segment of it, a segment which in my opinion has one of the brightest futures of any section of our development, has been waiting for many years for politicians to quit playing around with agriculture and to start doing something for the agriculturists. I am quite happy to admit that the previous government did a number of things for agriculture. Some of them worked, some did not. Some of them were advantageous to the farmer and some were detrimental. I think this government has already done some things for agriculture which have been advantageous, and they may do some more. They will also do some things not in the interest of the Canadian farmer.

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
We have heard a great deal of talk in recent days about sales which have been made. I think the time for politicians to quit playing around with sales of agricultural products arrived a long time ago. The time is long overdue that we cease regarding agricultural sales abroad as plums for one political party or another. Over the years we have developed through the wheat board an agency which has done an excellent job selling our agricultural produce and which has worked within the political confines of the government of the day. It has done an admirable job. The fact that we have sold this wheat is not to the credit of either the Liberal party or the Conservative party. It is to the credit of the wheat board, whose organization has been developed over many years. We should all be very satisfied that such a situation exists and that these sales have been made, because otherwise Canadians in many walks of life would have faced an extremely hard winter this year. But we were fortunate in having a large crop and in finding a market for that crop through the Canadian wheat board, with the result that many thousands of dollars which would not otherwise have been available to the industrial workers and the professional people of Canada will flow into, the resources of. this nation, the result of the efforts of our farmers who produced this wealth at the source.
I believe that agriculture has a bright future, I think it has a bright future despite governments, rather than because of them. We have a terrific potential. Over the years we have been able to increase the production of any agricultural commodity at relatively little cost except for the land and equipment required. How many other nations are able to increase their capacity, to produce by 25 per cent in a given agricultural commodity each 15 or 20 years? Yet we find this happening, and I think this does give us a great future.
As to the present agricultural situation it is, in my opinion, a grim one. Each year the average age of our farmers increases by one year. There are few young people entering the industry. This is a position we had better face. We should be making some provision for the future in terms, of the people who will be needed to make possible the development of our resources in the agricultural field. As all hon. members know, it costs a great deal of money to enter agriculture today. Even in the east a great deal of capital is required to secure a farm which will provide a decent standard of living, in addition to sufficient income for the repayment of a mortgage. I think an investment in the neighbourhood of $40,000 or $50,000 would probably be required. This might not amount

to much in the eyes, of farmers in western Canada who talk in terms of 5,000 acres and the equipment necessary to manage large tracts of land, but if I am right in the estimate I have made, and if it costs a young farmer $45,000 to acquire a farm which would provide him with a decent standard of living, I think he would find it a heck of a lot better to put that $45,000 into some other industry.
In these circumstances it is up to us to stop playing petty politics and get down to helping agriculturists of this country to establish a strong industry, an industry which people will be happy to enter. This has not been the situation under either of the former governments. It seems to me we must establish a more effective way of making farm loans. It is all very well for the government to say that the present arrangement is a success. I think it is working far better than did the old farm credit board. The terms are better, and the training of. the personnel has been improved. But we all know of many applications which have been turned down because, in order to make his venture financially possible, the applicant would have to supplement his income by wages earned off the farm. This moonlighting has caused great difficulties, not only in the field of farm credit but also in the labour sphere, difficulties which are obviously detrimental to the development of a healthy agricultural economy.
This was mentioned by the mover of the amendment. He said that in many areas it was impossible to get work done on the farms. This very situation affects the young people with whom we should be concerning ourselves. If a worker in a town wants to buy a hundred acres on the edge of a town for the sake of becoming a gentleman farmer in a small way, there is no need to design the whole of our agriculture policy around him. Our main purpose should be to design a policy to assist those who wish to enter upon agricultural production on a full time basis. We should make it possible for all such people to farm without having to seek employment outside.
One of the main reasons for the high cost of farm production today is the cost of farm machinery. I sat on the agriculture committee a few years ago when we considered this whole question. I think we conducted one of the most exhaustive studies which has been made of this subject. The former minister of agriculture cannot take any credit for the operations of the agriculture committee under his jurisdiction, because of his failure to implement any of the reasonable demands which were made by that committee for a reduction of the cost of farm machinery. I should like to mention one or two of the

recommendations which we made. One of them had to do with standardization, so that a John Deere tractor could be backed into a Massey Harris implement and tow an International harvester. We wanted the nuts and bolts and other attachments made standard so that this would be possible. We mentioned such things as the removal of cigarette lighters from tractors; such things as having the agricultural implements themselves made more practical and more basic; we referred to the need for having the machines thoroughly tested before they were allowed to reach the agricultural scene. All the members of the committee were united, I think, in the belief that something should be done on behalf of the farmers. But what happened? The cabinet pays no attention to any recommendation which comes from a committee of this house, and in this respect there was no difference between the recommendations which were made by the committee on agriculture or by any other committee, whether set up under the former government or under the present administration. We are doing as much good in the agriculture committee today, despite the fact the committee has not been called, as we were when we sat under the Tories. We are ruled in this country by the cabinet and the representations of backbenchers, particularly in a majority government, do not carry any weight.
The cost of farm machinery is probably one of the major costs of farming in western Canada, and even in eastern Canada the cost of buying machinery to meet the need for automation represents a large part of a farmer's expenditure. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) may not know it, but if a farmer were setting up a dairy farm in eastern Ontario today, milking cows would be a very small part of his job. Fixing the milking machine would be a much more important chore. He would no longer be cleaning the stables with a fork. He would clean them with a very simple but very expensive piece of machinery which would hose them, and still retain the valuable by-product. Every piece of equipment is very expensive, but in this small field of barn cleaners we have not been able to effect an economy.
There are others. We should not go around the country asking the farmers to produce more if we are not willing to sell what is produced. If anybody is to be given credit, I think the former minister of agriculture must be given some credit for at least making a good fight in the export market. It seems to me that we have been able to develop export markets, and I think he deserves some credit in this field because it was his job to make the general public aware of the fact that we need to sell.
