I used to be shocked by the attitude of a former minister of agriculture who had something to do with the sale of some of our commodities and who used to say: We have the best products and everybody knows it, so if they want to buy them let them come and buy them. In my opinion this is no way to sell our products, because it has been proven that you have to go out and sell them.
We can produce almost any agricultural product in abundance in Canada. The farmer, if he is given a year or two, can increase by 40 per cent his production of anything he is now producing, whether it be milk or any other commodity.
What are we going to do with these products? We have only one dairy product that we can sell without doing any work. We could sell more Canadian cheddar cheese on the export market tomorrow if it were produced, but the agricultural experts of this country will not ask the farmers to produce unpasteurized Canadian cheddar cheese that could be sold in the United Kingdom market. There is a shortage of that product every year. But what do the agricultural experts say? Produce more pasteurized cheddar cheese, a product that cannot be sold to most of our customers.
We could search out markets for most of our commodities. I think it is interesting to note that when the farmers themselves have had the courage to do this they have been able to assist greatly in the marketing of their products. In my area two or three farmers in two communities have set up community sales barns. This is a field that is very familiar to the minister, and maybe he can give some assistance in expanding it. Auction sales are conducted in these community sales barns, and in my area which is 350 to 400 miles from Toronto I find that the price we get is probably not more than two cents below the Toronto stockyard price.
The minister has been talking about feed grains. He ought to think about this, because our cattle are usually not fattened on grain: They are fattened in the pasture. Oh, yes, in the last few weeks we feed them, but we have many sources of feed available for cattle. We can use green fodder, we can use silage, we can use corn. There are many things that can fatten these cattle. If what is suggested is accomplished, then I suggest that the former minister of agriculture had better take a look around eastern Canada because he may find that the advantage the western producer has of having a product for feeding his cattle readily will no longer be an advantage, and there may not be so

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking many people return from western Canada because the situation may change almost overnight.
The same thing has also been accomplished in a small way by the hog producers of Ontario. They have co-operated to sell their products, and have been able to bring about some stability not by asking for government help, not by asking for their share of subsidization, but rather they have been able to accomplish in sales what the government with a subsidy failed to do over a long time.
If anyone will look at what subsidization has cost Canada he will find it is not a small thing. In the annual report for 1962-63 we see that it has amounted to $461 million. This is a sizeable sum of money and a lot of it has gone into butter production. I listened very attentively the other day to the statement the minister made with regard to the consumer subsidy placed on butter in order to sell it. We have tried to give it away. We have tried to store it. We have tried to convert it into oil and we have tried to pay consumers to buy it.
We spent $42 million in the period from April 30, 1962 to March 31, 1963 in this field. What did it do? I am told we are now eating more butter than we ever did before, because it is being used in the soft ice cream field and that a very large percentage of consumer supported butter has gone into hard ice cream. The ice cream in my area is considered about the best in Canada and I know that most of it is produced with the addition of butter under this program.
I suppose it does not matter what you do with the butter. I had a request from a businessman who wanted to buy butter oil for which I do not think there is any reasonable use. He wanted to buy it at seven or eight cents a quart so that he could help the government, pointing out that he would use it in his company to make bath oil. His comment was: "After all, Cleopatra used it, so we see no reason why we cannot buy this stuff at seven or eight cents a quart to make bath oil which the consumer will use, if it is properly perfumed." People talk about what detergents are doing to our sewage systems. I wonder what butter by the gallon draining out of bathtubs would do to the septic tank systems of municipalities throughout the nation?
We have tried everything except selling these products. If the government would take as much interest in selling them as they take credit for every increase that normally comes about by reason of the expansion of population in Canada and the additional consumption arising from increased wealth and a greater gross national product, I think they


would be doing something worth while. The people of Canada are looking to parliament for a long term solution of our problems. The only solution put forward to date, and it will have to stand until something better is suggested, is the ARDA program. I see it is almost six o'clock and I just want to mention that if the government think they are going to be able to do the same thing with ARDA that they did with P.F.R.A. in western Canada, and make it into a political patronage machine, they have got another think coming. I would rather see the ARDA program scuttled in eastern Canada than to see it develop into a monster like P.F.R.A. was in western Canada, in terms of the patronage that has gone with it. I think this is a program that could work but it is not going to work if applied in any political way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the supper adjournment I had mentioned the ARDA program. It is the only long term agricultural program introduced in recent years that would appear to many people, and I am one of them, to present a long term solution for the agricultural problems of the nation. I do not want to see this program turned into a patronage machine like so many others have been, including P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A., both of which have been used by governments in power to spread political propaganda and patronage. ARDA should certainly be operated at a higher level than that.
When it was first outlined ARDA, according to the resources for tomorrow committee, had three main objectives:	First, to develop
alternative uses for land classified as marginal or of low productivity; second, to develop income and employment opportunities for rural agricultural areas; third, to develop and conserve the water and soil resources of Canada. I do not think any one would disagree with any of these objectives.
The first thing we should do is provide the most effective use for the available land we have, and certainly we do not need to travel far outside of Ottawa to see the abuses to which our land has been subjected. Some 40 or 50 years ago huge timber stands were to be found in the Ottawa valley, but now there are only very limited amounts of Cyprus cedars, where at one time the area was richly productive in white pine. This land will never be really productive again. In most cases the

top soil covering the rocks is too thin to be of value, but where we run into difficulty is in deciding what to do with this land.
Some people say that the land should be turned over to ARDA for development and let the government reforest it, or let somebody manage and operate it in some other way. Others say they should get advantage of it now. They say, "Let us sell our broken down, worn out land and get a good price from the government for it. If I have voted right and know the right people maybe my farm will be the one someone will buy." This, of course, is the political factor involved in any long term program, but I suggest it should not be the guiding factor.
This may not be true of other provinces, but in Ontario many people have been looking on the ARDA program as a new milk cow from which they can get milk in a very easy stream from the federal government. This is not what I contemplate ARDA to be, and it is not what was contemplated by the resources for tomorrow committee. Here is what that committee said of ARDA in regard to provincial co-operation:
All of the provinces have agreed In principle to co-operative federal-provincial action under ARDA. It would appear that three things are necessary if it is to function for the greatest benefit:
1.	That programs be established with adequate consideration for all uses of all renewable resources.
2.	That planning have the benefit of a national survey of the land and its productive capacities under the guidance of members of various professions (the soil scientist, the economist, the plant and animal scientists, the forester, the engineer). This will require a high degree of co-operation between governments and between several departments of any one government.
3.	That local and municipal organizations take the maximum possible action initiative; that they participate fully in planning programs and putting them into effect.
I suggest one of the things that should have happened under ARDA is that a national survey should have been taken to establish all the land of a marginal nature, and to discover what renewable resources could be produced from it. Such a survey might have taken a year or two, but it would have provided the blueprint for the program. Such a survey would involve a lot of work and energy, and maybe the Minister of Agriculture has not got the capacity to organize it; but if we continue to look for day to day projects that will bring votes we will never realize the agricultural potential of the nation. To do that a survey such as this is necessary.
There are a great number of projects under consideration right now that do not fit into the program of a national survey. I imagine that sometime in the next five or six years a government will come out with a scheme for such a survey in order to put ARDA on the 28902-5-227i
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking proper track, where it should have been in the beginning, so that we may know what developments should take place, and in what areas, for the greatest benefit of the nation.
It should not matter whether someone is paid for his farm on the basis of reforestation, or whether the farm should be used for grazing, and so on. A survey would establish what is the best land use. I think this is the prime consideration in the success of the ARDA program. What will become of ARDA remains to be seen. There are many Canadians in the rural economy of this country who are not particularly interested in ARDA, because today the average age of the farmer is over 60 and he is not looking for us to plant trees on his farm. He does not really care what happens to the farm across the road. He wants a decent standard of living today in the profession to which he has devoted his life.
I think this is where governments are involved. The farmer can produce whatever the government suggests. I think this has been admirably shown in what has happened to wheat. Probably this is a very fortunate accident, rather than intention. It really is not the government's fault that there was a crop failure in Russia, or that there has been a famine in China for the past three years. These are facts of nature and these sales really cannot be put to the credit of the Department of Agriculture and its officials. We are very fortunate that these events have taken place, as far as our sales of wheat are concerned. I think it behooves us, even in the field of wheat, to design our program so we will know how much wheat to produce and how much our long term markets will require. I think we also have to establish in Canada a large reserve of wheat against the day when there is a need for this reserve in order to keep alive the people of the world. If I were familiar with the Bible I could probably quote the passage that talks about the planning of storage in the early days in Egypt, when they had the wheat stored in their granaries and were able to give it to those nations surrounding them in order to preserve the very life of those nations. We may find ourselves in that position. It may be necessary to survey the needs of the world in relation to the amount that Canada can produce. It will not really do us much good to change much of the agricultural land that we now have that is in reasonable production, until we know what our potential is and what the needs of the world are. Every year there is going to be a greater market for our agricultural produce. I do not know whether the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) can say the same of his department. I am not sure that we are going to need to produce more cars in Canada, or more textiles, than

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking we produce today. But I am sure that because of the geographical location of Canada we will need a greater production of agricultural products. The only thing our governments have to do is find out how we are going to dispose of this production.
I think the government is to be commended, both this government and the previous one, in what they have been able to do for wheat. We will not go into the question of why they were able to do it. Let us give them full credit for that. But I wonder what we are going to do with some of the other things we are producing. This government and the previous one have shamefully neglected the milk production industry of this nation. They either know nothing about it or they have not done anything about what they do know. The milk producers came to Ottawa several years ago and asked for the right to blend their price. They came to Ottawa later and asked for the right to put a five cent levy on fluid milk producers and for help in subsidizing the sale of cheese. What did the government do? Absolutely nothing. They waited until there was no need for the subsidy and the problem had already reached the position where the industry itself could not agree. Now there is a need for planning in regal'd to all milk, because farmers producing milk should be given the opportunity of disposing of that commodity at a fair and reasonable price. This has been highly accelerated in parts of Canada, particularly in Ontario, where there are scientific developments in the production of fluid milk and we are producing commodities such as multimilk, and so on, which are cutting into the sales of fluid milk to a great extent. It is true that this is a secondary milk product. It could be put in the class of manufactured milk, but when the end product is reconstituted into whole fluid milk it takes an expert to detect the difference between the two products.
Therefore I suggest that in this field if in no other the government will have to give assistance to the industry. The federal Department of Agriculture should be giving some advice and leadership as to how to solve this particular problem. Why ask the federal government to do it? Mr. Speaker, who is better qualified to assess the needs of the nation than the federal government. What do we find? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) challenges somebody who may never have been on a dairy farm to milk cows. I ask the house, is that a very high level of debate? I certainly think that Canada is in need of leadership in this field. We have a great need in this area. We will support the Minister of Agriculture in any reasonable agricultural policy, no matter which political party brings it forward; but


I think we have the obligation as a federal government to convene immediately the agriculture committee and sit down and decide some of the answers to these problems affecting agriculture. I suggest that this amendment will be a very small thing in eastern Canada, considering that we have many other problems.
I also suggest that the committee sit down and solve some of these problems, and after hours and hours of working on a particular problem the government has an obligation to the committee to at least listen to its recommendations. If the government says it does not want to do anything about them, let them at least have the guts to have the Minister of Agriculture inform parliament that they are going to disagree and are not giving any consideration to the report of the committee. I have been here for four parliaments and have heard my colleagues continually saying, "What a wonderful thing, these committees. Let us concentrate more on committees". I agree with them, but in view of my experience of the past one might as well save one's time going to a committee meeting, because when the report is made, what happens? It is laid on the table, and I defy anybody to tell me what is done with it, except to store it in the archives for our successors to read and be amused by some of our solutions.
Therefore I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture to give some honest consideration to the problems of eastern Canada. We have always helped those in western Canada to solve their problems, and we in eastern Canada are in dire need of assistance today in the agricultural field. The farmers are not going ahead; they are going backwards. One does not see new farmers today; we take all the old farmers to the cemetery. Farms in my part of the country are left neglected, because no one can go into farming as a young person today and make a success of it. I do not think it is a very creditable commentary on the situation in Canada when we have this need, we have the ability and yet do nothing to bring these two things together and try to effect a solution. It may be, as one member of parliament said, "We have the gravel; we have the cement; we have the water. Why haven't we got the sidewalks?" I think in this case it is not necessary that we have these problems. We spend a great deal of money on other things. We have the know-how, but we need advice and direction, and this we are not getting from our Department of Agriculture, to solve or attempt to solve many of these problems that have been with us for some time and are today crying out for a solution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with sustained interest to the motion brought in by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). In my opinion, it was quite a performance on his part to succeed in describing so vividly in so short a time the situation of agriculture in eastern Canada.
Such words are not out of place in the mouth of the former Minister of Agriculture whose inaction caused agriculture to deteriorate in the space of a few short years in eastern Canada. Who could have been better chosen than him to stress in the house the lot of eastern farmers whose standard of living is undeniably lower than that of other farmers in Canada?
The first part of his remarks was a normal introduction to the second part of his speech where he tried to prove that the present government did not succeed to improve the conditions of farmers in a few months.
I will come back to that later on but I should like to point out now that the problem facing eastern agriculture is a very concrete one which must be acknowledged before any solution is sought.
Any political measure, either in the field of agriculture or in any other area of public life, must first be based on a precise and accurate appraisal of the situation. First, we
all know what the situation of eastern Canadian farmers is in relation to modern progress. We realize that his standard of living places him in an impossible situation compared to the population as a whole. We see various craftsmen, professionals improving their lot, their financial status, but on the other hand, the farmer living on a small farm does not share in this progress. He is aware of this, he is unhappy about it and he has been crying for help for many years.
And it took a party like ours, a government like ours, to understand the grief of the small eastern farmer.
His grief is psychological. He needs to feel that the government is behind him, and that is exactly what the present government wanted to achieve in introducing here a measure to enable one of its members to occupy another agriculture portfolio. That need of the farmer to see his lot improved, to feel he is supported in a growing economy, is based on a certain fact and an important one, the standard of living of the eastern farmer in relation to that of farmers in the country as a whole.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle gave some figures. I will go over them and I think no one will be able to contradict such a clearcut situation.
Whereas in 1962, the farmers' net income in the whole of the maritimes, excluding Quebec, totalled $901, in Quebec, it amounted to $1,659 whereas in the western provinces, in Alberta for instance, a farmer earned $4,052 and in the prairies as a whole, excluding British Columbia, $4,011.
If those figures are compared with those in other groups, one finds that the eastern farmer, in the maritimes, Quebec and Ontario, finds himself in the most unbearable situation. It is because he feels the need to improve his living standard that he looks for solutions.
How could the government settle the problem of an inadequate standard of living for the farmer by comparison with other groups of the society? It can contribute to increase the price of his products and services or to reduce his production cost.
Unfortunately, it seems to me that we were too anxious in the past to solve the problem of insufficient farm income by granting repeated increases in the prices of products without making allowance for the consequences on the market of that steady increase in support prices.
More and more-and this is a policy the present government must apply-the farmer's production cost will have to be reduced. And that reduction shall come through improving the farmer's efficiency on his farm. In fact, it has been said for a long time that the farmer, on his small farm, does not have
3560	HOUSE OF
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking all the necessary technical knowledge to be efficient and place on the market a product which can be compared to those of the larger farm units.
That is why the federal government, in cooperation with the provinces, feels that it is essential to increase the technical knowledge made available to the farmers. In fact, in the whole eastern part of the country, the experimental farm system will soon be completely reorganized; these farms are precisely designed to make available to the farmer all the latest technical discoveries, the most improved products in order to increase his efficiency and therefore reduce his cost of production.
Besides, the farmer's efficiency will improve through a more rational use of farm machinery. In that respect, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) indicated a few moments ago the concern of the experts in finding methods allowing the small land owner to use in a more efficient and economical way the very costly farm machinery which he also needs, but for which he often cannot afford to pay the monthly instalments.
Production cost could also be cut down by the adoption of a new feed grain policy which would make it possible to breed cattle more economically in eastern Canada. I will have more to say about that later on.
An inadequate standard of living is not the only problem facing many eastern farmers.
A second problem is that of income instability. In fact, not only has the eastern farmer a lower income than other Canadians, but his income changes from year to year so that, at one time, he may get into debt for his farm or for his family and then, later on, he finds himself heavily indebted towards lending companies when he has no money to meet his obligations.
This instability has also a psychological effect on the farmer. Living in a world which requires more and more security and finds it in measures of stabilization enacted by the government, the farmer feels insecure owing to the large fluctuations in his income from one year to the other.
How can we help in reducing these fluctuations of income, this instability in the farmer's income? The experience that our fellow farmers in the west have known will have to be tried differently in many fields of production in eastern Canada. During many conferences on agricultural matters, the provinces have agreed to co-operate with the federal government in the establishment of joint organizations for the marketing in an orderly and stable way of various farm commodities produced on eastern Canada farms.


It would be of no avail for the federal and the provincial governments to pass the buck as far as responsibilities in farm products stabilization are concerned. The time when each could, in its own area, attempt to find a solution to the problem is a thing of the past. More and more, we must find methods of co-operation in the area of farm products stabilization. And the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) did set oil that co-operation in a very effective way at the last conference held in Edmonton.
And that co-operation is proceeded with, specially in the east, in order to set up stabilization and price support organizations which will prevent too sharp variations which were so disastrous for our eastern producers in the past.
The third problem facing the eastern farmer is brought about because he feels so destitute in the face of the tremendous resources the economy enjoys in other sectors while he is still at a primitive farming stage and cannot keep pace with the progress all around him.
Would the solution in that field be the isolation of the eastern agriculture in a kind of ivory tower which could bring about some stability except for relations with the rest of the country and even with the rest of the world? I do not think so. Indeed, I think that in the past too much was done to isolate our eastern agriculture from the whole economy of the country and from all international markets.
The benefits of competition must extend to all areas of agriculture, and international markets as well as the whole domestic market must be made increasingly available to those small producers who often find themselves at a loss when faced with the big economic task they have to achieve.
Faced with those three problems, what does the present government have to offer? What achievements has it already got on the credit side and what lead may be expected from it to deal with agricultural problems in the eastern part of the country?
As for the initial step the government has decided to take, there is a resolution on the order paper and the house will soon be called upon to study a measure setting up, within the Department of Agriculture, a double direction.
I do not intend to dwell upon this problem as we shall have the opportunity, while studying the bill, to point out the beneficial consequences that such a double direction will bring about for the eastern producers in general.
The intention expressed here is not to divide but to unite, so as to get a better management of the country's agricultural business. For once, we want the eastern

farmer to feel himself bound to all the other farmers, so that, with two men working together, we may see, for the first time in this country, the agricultural field as prosperous as other spheres of our economy.
With regard to the stabilization policy, more particularly in the dairy field, the house has already been informed, Mr. Speaker, of the significant legislation this government introduced when it came into office, in order to get away from the concept of the former administration, which had to grant perpetual increases for milk and butter, and was left with a considerable surplus on its hands. This government has got away from that concept and tried to find among the dairy produce markets those who would absorb considerable quantities.
We easily discovered-because it had been demonstrated in several years of inertia on the part of the former administration-that we had to turn away from butter and go into the considerable market for cheese.
Our stabilization policy, which has been in force since May 1, resulted in a considerable decrease in butter production and more particularly-as was intended-in the increase of cheese production by approximately 16 per cent, without having to face any surplus problem, because all that production has already been sold abroad.
Such a dairy policy precisely illustrates how to approach a solution of our farm problems which would duly consider the future of our national and international markets while getting away from old concepts of politics, which had been applied for a long time to our farmers.
In matters of education or technical training, what positive steps has this government taken up to now to help the eastern farmer improve his knowledge in agricultural matters?
Reorganization of the education on farming subjects has already been decided on, so that a centralization can be developed within each eastern province and so that such knowledge, contrary to what was done in the past, can be disseminated in all farming areas through the setting up of experimental farms which will continually get their material from those research centres. In turn, they will be in a position to supply the farmers with technical and other knowledge they need to raise the level of efficiency of that production.
I said that this government was more interested in the reduction of farm production costs for eastern farmers than in an artificial increase of the price of those products. It is in relation to such a policy that the present Minister of Agriculture announced a new feed grain policy some time ago.
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
All those who have studied the problems of agriculture in the east know that one of the most expensive items for the farmer is the purchase of feed grain for cattle during the long winter months when the harsh weather makes it impossible to use the grazing grounds.
In order to prevent an artificial rise in price for such feed grain during the winter, we have set up some policies designed first to pay the cost of storing the feed during the winter in order not to penalize those who have to keep large stocks of feed and who, consequently, had a tendency to transfer those higher prices during the winter to the eastern farmers.
That policy whereby storage costs are paid was followed by another which has been announced and will be explained in detail within a few days; it is a new policy to help the transportation of feed grain to eastern Canada.
As we know, this policy was the work of a Liberal administration, of a Liberal government; but it had to be renewed in the light of experience and new problems which faced us. It is because of changes in the methods of transport that the new policy concerning payment of freight charges for grain will be carried out.
This policy will consist in paying the basic price, the price of transport by water, to which will be added, as the case may be, the extra transportation costs by train or by truck, for the basic ports as far as the various areas determined for that purpose.
The result will be: first, to standardize within an area the various prices of grain, and second, to allow fair competition between the various means of transport. We hope that these will help to reduce freight costs on the shipping of these grains to eastern Canada. Finally, a third feature of our grain policy is the establishment of deferred payments.
Contrary to the system which existed under the previous administration, those buying grain at the lakehead would only pay the price which will be in force at the time of delivery, so that the middlemen will not have to take unnecessary chances on account of price variation and, as in the past, to reduce the grain stocks available for eastern farmers.
We want to point out that those three measures, which have already been announced, are not just promises for the future. We believe that they will improve tremendously the price level situation and the variation in feed grain prices in the whole eastern part of our country, and will therefore decrease the cost of production for our eastern farmers.

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
Now, many questions have been asked since the beginning of this session, and also a while ago about the ARDA program. It has been asked whether the present government intends to maintain that program which was introduced by the previous government, following numerous studies initiated in the Senate under the previous government, by a very intensive investigation of the use of land in eastern Canada.
We have always thought and we still think that technical measures must be set up for farmers who live in what is called submarginal conditions, that is farmers who perhaps do not have all the technical and economic means to succeed on their farms, either because the land is not fit for farming or because the markets are too far away, or because the environment is not adequate for a certain type of farming.
We must consider converting certain marginal farms to more profitable uses under ARDA. A program such as the one embodied in ARDA can allow us to set up, in particular areas, efficient programs which will benefit the people living there.
Many important studies concerning redevelopment and rehabilitation must be made before government legislation is enacted. That is why the Minister of Agriculture has urged every province in particular to co-operate with him in carrying out research in various parts of eastern and western Canada, in order precisely to discover within those regions in what manner submarginal lands could be put to better use. Those studies are proceeding satisfactorily and as they are completed, the federal government, in co-operation with the province, will be able to set up very effective programs for the reconversion of those lands so as to improve the standard of living in the areas concerned.
The purpose of ARDA and the Agricultural Stabilization Act would not be achieved if we failed to tackle the problem of credit. We realized very soon, as the Minister of Agriculture pointed out this afternoon, that in many cases the amounts made available to eastern farmers by the Farm Credit Corporation were insufficient to permit the proper development of many undertakings that bring in a high income in various areas. Therefore, officials of the Farm Credit Corporation have been asked to conduct a detailed survey, by region and by type of farming, on those basic needs, which the corporation would have been unable to meet in the past, so that we can adjust to those various needs.
The study is still going on and the Minister of Agriculture will soon be able to recommend changes most likely to help eastern farmers

to renew their equipment, improve their farms and extend their markets for various agricultural products.
As was often pointed out, too much stress may have been put on milk production in eastern Canada. It was a mistake not to show more interest in cattle breeding in the past, considering the vast markets which were to be found in Toronto, Montreal and the other large centres in eastern Canada. It is because of our awareness of the problem that the Minister of Agriculture has set up within his department a special committee which is to formulate a policy concerning livestock breeding in the eastern part of the country and whose recommendations will be forwarded to the house in due time for the improvement of breeding conditions in eastern Canada.
In our part of the country, farmers are looking for more diversified production while a vast market is being supplied, at least in part, through livestock imports. We should, therefore, establish once and for all a policy to promote development in that important sector of agriculture.
All the steps I have mentioned would not have helped solve the problem of eastern agriculture if the Minister of Agriculture and his officials had failed to realize the importance of setting up and maintaining international markets for our various farm products-those of the west which are doing remarkably well, and those of the east. Demand requires contacts with the United States and various European countries interested in buying certain crops they lack while we have surpluses. It is still partly with such a policy in mind that the Minister of Agriculture has visited various European countries, in order precisely to look into the possibility of co-operating in this field and exporting also our different agricultural products on those markets.
Mr. Speaker, this brief sketch of the problems which existed when this government came to power and the action which we have already taken or which are under consideration for the near future, well indicate that this government has no greater concern than to help efficiently the eastern farmer to solve his problems in order that the stagnation which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle pointed out, when introducing his motion and looking back on his administration, may disappear as quickly as possible in eastern Canada.
Finally, I hope that eastern farmers who in the past have felt neglected and powerless in the face of modern economic phenomena, may at last feel for the first time that a Canadian government, their government, is considering their problems and is finding appropriate

solutions. It will thus have contributed to rehabilitate the people who have been so deserving in the past throughout the country and who are only seeking redress. They are asking the state to consider their problems; this is exactly what the present government has done since it came into power and it is exactly what the Minister of Agriculture is doing. I hope that in the very near future, I will be in a position to help him to perform that task and to co-operate with him in the best interests of our eastern farmers.

In addition, the former minister of agriculture had put on the order paper an important bill concerning the transportation of western grain to eastern Canada, but as soon as a great number of members of the opposition realized that the bill was to help the farmers, the same as other bills, like the one amending the Farm Credit Act and ARDA, they defeated the government.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute publicly to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for presenting this bill, following many weeks of study, in order to provide an increased income for the eastern farmers of our country.
Mr. Speaker, as previously mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, 100,000 families receive at the present time an inadequate farm income and they appeal to this government to help them out of their financial difficulties. At the present time, there is at the national level an imbalance which puts confederation in jeopardy. When a group of citizens within a country are at a disadvantage, when their incomes are inadequate, the rest of the citizens are also affected and this contributes to widen the gap economically speaking and even to put national unity in jeopardy.
There is a national imbalance since 43 per cent of the eastern farmers live on marginal or submarginal land; moreover, labour, fertilizer and farm machinery now cost more. The problems are many.
The situation in the dairy industry is unstable. Tomorrow an expert in that field, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent), will deal with that matter in detail.
Mr. Speaker, I do not share the views expressed by the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane. He spoke about a new policy regarding the dairy industry. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the eastern farmers were happier with the payment of 25 cents per hundredweight of milk to be processed than with the government's new policy.

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
We should keep in mind that from 1959 to 1963, the policy launched by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle brought in nearly $50 million to eastern farmers, and when we asked the Minister of Agriculture No. 1 why the government had abolished that policy, he answered: "In order to save $6 million". That is just to show how much he was aware of the eastern farmer's problem.
The government should not forget that there are problems in the dairy and tobacco industries. I know that several hon. members from Ontario realize that there are several million pounds of cigarette tobacco yet unsold, and an over-production of cigarette tobacco in the province of Quebec. We would like to know what the Minister of Agriculture did when he went to Russia, and elsewhere and also whether he found a way to sell a few pounds of tobacco to pay for his journey, which was financed by Canadian taxpayers.
There is also a considerable decrease in apple sales.
We should, moreover, increase our subsidies to federal experimental farms in the east, and more particularly, in the province of Quebec.
I wonder whether the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane knows that all agronomists are leaving the experimental farm of L'Assomption. I would urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), to better working conditions, if possible, so that agronomists and agricultural technicians remain in the federal experimental stations of eastern Canada to carry on their research work, as the farm revenue is so low there.
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis), who is not in his seat, is laughing. I am dealing with an important matter and the Postmaster General should be more serious and listen to what I am saying.
When I was parliamentary secretary to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, we wanted, by all possible means, to draw here, in Ottawa, in the federal Department of Agriculture, many French speaking agronomists and agricultural technicians, because, at the present time, there are very few bilingual experts at the Ottawa experimental farm, under the Department of Agriculture, so that French Canadian farmers whose farming income is very low cannot communicate easily with the federal authorities, and cannot be conversant with the federal acts which could help them to increase their income.
I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture should ask graduates of the agricultural school of Laval University to spend two or three days in Ottawa so as to show them how


to secure a position in the Department of Agriculture for, if we sincerely want our eastern farmers to benefit, if we want them to have their share of the national revenue, it is essential to improve the channels of communication between the federal Department of Agriculture and eastern farmers.
I strongly urge the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane-I see that he has just left his seat, he is probably not very interested in that problem-I urge him to meet the minister of agriculture of the province of Quebec as soon as possible. A long time ago, I spoke about it myself to the Quebec minister of agriculture, in the hope of bringing about a program of crop insurance beneficial to Quebec farmers, particularly to those among them who specialize in a given type of crop; like our tobacco growers for instance.
Our farmers badly need an insurance of that kind; for them, it is practically a question of life and death. They cannot do without crop insurance. Federal legislation is a great help, as it covers 50 per cent of administration costs, and 20 per cent of the premiums paid.
Mr. Speaker, tobacco producers for cigarettes and cigars have invested considerable sums in their business, in order to see it prosper; however, they do not know whether they will be able to recover their capital. Insecurity is nothing new to them, for they have, only too often, been victimized by frost, rain, drought, and so forth.
I would ask the present Minister of Agriculture to hurry up and get in touch with provincial authorities in order to help the farmers of eastern Canada as soon as possible, because his future assistant or colleague does not seem interested in those problems.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) made a speech which amounted to a statement of policy. Now, as you know, the hon. member is an economist and some economists remind me of certain psychiatrists. Under the latter's care, the patient often gets worse. And I would not care to see the situation of eastern farmers get worse under an economist like the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane.
As a matter of fact, that is what we are afraid of on this side of the house.
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane knew his bill would be brought forward in the house soon and that he would probably be appointed minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, during the summer recess why did he choose to go to Malaysia instead of taking this opportunity to visit farmers of eastern Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, and experimental farms in

those provinces and to knock on the farmers' doors in order to find out all about their problems?
Malaysia is not the place to find out about those particular problems. And newspapermen have taken the minister to task for those very things I am telling him now. In fact, the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane was not being serious. He should have taken advantage of the recess to brush up on farm problems. If he had done so, I am convinced that he would not have made the statement of policy that we heard this evening, when he merely indicated some of the farm problems.
Mr. Speaker, we, on this side of the house, have been aware for a long time of the problems facing the eastern farmer. That is why the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) tackled them and visited the province of Quebec in order to become familiar with them. Following this visit, he had placed on the order paper, a motion providing for an increase in the farmers' income.
Unfortunately, we lost the election and we have not been able to implement that legislation.
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Agriculture smiles, we find it difficult not to smile ourselves.
However, for the information of the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane, may I give the results of the survey made by the caisses populaires and the welfare agencies of lower St. Lawrence valley.
The farm situation of the lower St. Lawrence valley, where the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane lives, is typical of that in Abitibi and even in Lake St. John district, except for the lake belt.
The brief divides the population into average farmers, small farmers, day labourers living on old farms, settlers and foresters; the first manage to live on $2,000, but what about the others?
And to show you an example of a family of the lower St. Lawrence valley, of Gaspe peninsula, here is an excerpt from the report:
Here is an example from a case considered by the agency:

In other words, Mr. Speaker, that farm is more than submarginal. It is but an example, but that situation somewhat reflects the farm situation in eastern Canada, and that is why eastern farmers would have liked to see the passage of the bill which was on the order paper when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was minister of agriculture, for that measure included many advantages.
As a matter of fact, it would have helped the transportation of western grain to eastern Canada and increase the farmers' income.
Mr. Speaker, here are some principles and facts that should be known concerning a mutual assistance policy on feed grain transportation in the east.
1.	There should be uniform and balanced prices throughout the east, so that no grain consumer will be at a disadvantage.
2.	There should at all times be a sufficient and reliable supply of grain available to all, everywhere throughout the year.
3.	There should be sufficient storage facilities available to satisfy the eastern consumer as well as the western producer.
4.	It is a well known fact that water transportation is by far the least costly, but unfortunately seasonal, so there should be reasonable decentralization of storage facilities.
5.	It is expected that by 1975, grain consumption will again increase by 50 per cent. Let us not forget that in 1960 it already amounted to 400 million bushels, 241 million being produced in the east while the rest came from the west. In general, 35 per cent of the feed grain is purchased by hog and other meat producers and two thirds are produced on the farm.
6.	Price fluctuations in different places and at different times represent a great difficulty indeed for producers. An adjustment of these conditions would be an important basic reform.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, there will surely be opposition to these measures in some circles.
It is extremely important that a bill be introduced as soon as possible for the storing of grain and its movement from western to eastern Canada. That would enable the early transformation of a raw material, grain, into finished products on eastern farms.

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking
Mr. Speaker, I should like to repeat here what I said recently. According to the Washington bureau of statistics, the United States will have a population of 300 million by 1980 and possibly 350 million by the turn of the century, that is less than 40 years from now. The population of Canada will not be stationary either. Meat consumption goes up as the population increases. As I said earlier, it is always better for a country like Canada to export raw material as fully processed as possible.
Now, when Canada exports a ton of barley, for instance, our economy is richer by approximately $50; in other words, Canada increases its foreign reserves by $50.
On the other hand, if that ton of barley in the raw state, is transformed into pork or beef in the east and the meat is exported, the same ton of barley brings $125 or more and becomes an additional source of income for the eastern farmer, benefiting at the same time to the economy of Canada as a whole.
In addition, if this product is processed in our country, jobs will be provided for the workers at a time when unemployment is a serious problem, and at least $75 per ton will be added to the international monetary fund which is depleted at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need to deal any longer with the beneficial effects for agriculture in eastern Canada of the legislation introduced by the former minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, if the house had given him the opportunity to carry it through.
In conclusion, I can think of no better instrument than a measure such as the one we introduced.
First, it would solve the problems of eastern farmers.
Second, it would provide the western producer with a firm market for his feed grain.
Third, that program would have contributed to strengthen the national economy by creating more jobs and permitting the export of a finished product instead of a raw material.
Fourth, that legislation would have contributed to provide for the future, which is the duty of any legislator aware of his responsibilities.
The policy of the present government, since it came into power, has been a failure, including the farm policy. The government has refused to assume its responsibilities.
I have here the 1962 platform of the Liberal party, which is certainly not very different from the 1963 version.
[Mr. Pigeon.1

Here is what we find:
Support of farm income
Improved price support system
Increased consumption of milk products
And a little further on, we read this:
A new Liberal government will initiate a national plan to promote better food habits, including the free distribution of milk in schools.
Mr. Speaker, during the summer recess, the two ministers of agriculture spent almost two months in Europe and Asia instead of approaching provincial authorities in order to arrive at an agreement which would not encroach on provincial autonomy, in connection with the consumption and distribution of milk in schools.
During an interview granted to a well-known newspaperman, the Minister of Agriculture No. 1 stated that he was interested in many things, but that he did not wish to discuss the appointment of two ministers of agriculture and the Canadian agricultural policy.
Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government is a failure and we urge the government to resign and call a general election, in order that, once and for all, the people may return to power a government which will ensure the prosperity of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened with attention to the future minister of agriculture for the east, who spoke after the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) who was also, at a certain time, aspirant to the office of minister of agriculture for the eastern provinces.
It is unfortunate that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm did not, at the time his party was in office, put forward the fine principles that he outlined tonight. In fact, it occurs to me that, in 1958, the Conservatives were holding exactly 208 seats in the Ottawa parliament. They remained in office for six years and the then minister of agriculture, as well as the aspirant minister, who has just resumed his seat, were not able to carry out any of the famous principles advocated tonight by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
If the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm had achieved only a quarter of what he outlined tonight, surely he would still be in office. In fact, if he is no longer
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking in office, it is because he never could translate his fine words into action at the time he had the power to do it; he never could accomplish anything.
We also listened to the remarks of the future minister of agriculture for eastern Canada and we heard him bewail, and rightly so, the fate of the Quebec farmers.
He stated that the Quebec farmers were in an untenable position. This is true. But he said a little later that the situation was merely psychological. Well, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Liberal party can find enough psychologists to settle the problem of the eastern farmers, because up to now, when anyone spoke of agriculture in this house, unfortunately, it was always about wheat. In my opinion, Canadian agriculture has much more significance and embodies much more than the simple matter of wheat, though this, we agree, is very important.
For the eastern farmers, we have butter, cheese, milk, millfeed, and feed grain, which has been mentioned in the house for only about a year.
It must be well remembered that last year, in this house, the then hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Dumont) raised an outcry, and I wish to point it out-he was the first to draw the attention of the hon. members to the fact that in eastern Canada, we have not the privilege of being able to buy our feed grain at normal prices.
I have here before me a bill from a cooperative society of ours, that is the agricultural co-operative society of Granby, according to which they bought-it is an example, by the way-wheat for $3.50 per hundred pounds; the bill amounts to $70.10 for 1,700 pounds of different millfeeds. Well, Mr. Speaker, it means that our eastern farmers have to pay about $4.25 per hundred pounds for millfeeds.
The Liberals and the Conservatives have been in power since confederation and the agricultural problems we have to face today have never been and shall never be solved so long as we do not take the proper and required means to correct these problems.
The farmer, in the twentieth century, is someone who has invested much capital and who face altogether many risks. He has invested capital on cattle, that is a living investment which, tomorrow, may be stricken, perhaps killed by some diseases.
Moreover, the farmers have invested much capital in their crops, which crops are subject to frost, wind, in brief to bad weather, or nature's whims and fancies.
After having ventured so much capital on machinery, crops, cattle, rolling stock and
35S8

Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking on the land itself, the farmer never knows the price he may get for his own production.
Presently, the eastern farmer in Canada is especially a slave to the trusts. He receives from them what they are willing to drop into his hat.
The farmers do an important job, they pursue a very hard profession, and they have proved it. They furnish a generous and good quality product in the country, but on the other hand, the more they produce, the more trouble they have to live. Why? Because they cannot solve a problem which is not their responsibility; they cannot solve the economic problem which confronts the farmers in our country.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mata-pedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay), who is said to be the future minister of agriculture in the eastern provinces, made a great statement of principles. He advocated cutting production costs for the eastern farmers. But he did not tell us which means he will use to reduce the prices. He did not say that the eastern farmers may buy wheat in their country at the same prices as the Russians have lately, that is about $1.50 the bushel, which is equivalent to about $2.50 the hundred pounds. Why do the Canadian farmers have to pay about $1 more than the Russians? Because they are presently the subjects and the slaves of the trusts, as I said a few minutes ago.
An election campaign was held last April during which a stable government was advocated. The Liberal party was returned to power. I believe that the people somewhat considered this slogan in returning the Liberal party to office.
Well, Mr. Speaker, a stable government would also mean a stable farm policy, stable prices, for the farmer who, at this time, sees not only the cost of his farm machinery and implements increase from day to day but also the price of meal and feed grain, while the produce he grows and puts on the market, does not increase, in proportion with what he has to buy.
I have here in my hand a copy of a farm paper, La Terre de Chez Nous, of October 2, 1963, which contains a statistical report by Mr. D. E. Grandpre under the title, "La clef des champs" or rather a synthesis of the taxes which farmers have to pay today, as well as the steady increase in taxation in the last few years.
The municipal real estate tax has increased by more than 200 per cent on Ontario farms in the last 13 or 14 years. The total was $13.9 million in 1946, whereas in 1959, the figure had reached $42.3 million. Yet, in the same period, the net farm

revenue was far from having risen in the same proportion of 200 per cent, but only increased by 29 per cent.
Which means that between the increased revenue and the increased taxes, there is a difference of exactly 171 per cent.
Those are the figures quoted by the federation of agriculture for that province.
A survey has also been made in the county of Restigouche-Madawaska, in New Brunswick, on the farmers' plight in that district.
If we glance over to our neighbour in eastern Quebec, we find the same conditions. Some 116 farmers who recently took a part in a survey in the county of Madawaska, unanimously stated that taxation is one of our main problems, if not the most important in their area.
The study was conducted by the federal rural economics division. The main results have just been published in the Farm Economist which is put out by that branch.
I think the Minister of Agriculture knows that publication. He should get some information on surveys made in the county, in order to settle those problems.
In the county of Madawaska, like elsewhere, and perhaps more than in other areas, municipal taxes have risen rapidly during the last few years. Around 1960 they represented 10.4 per cent of cash expenses on the 116 farms covered by the survey.
The figures quoted by one of our farmers give a pretty good idea of the additional charges brought about between 1951 and 1960. In that ten year period, the land tax climbed from $1.75 to $6.06 for every hundred dollars of assessment. The farm of the man I am speaking about, was assessed at $6,900; he paid $480 in land taxes in 1960, that's to say $342 more in yearly tax, according to the given assessment.
Well, in his speech, the future minister of agriculture for our eastern regions said not a word about the taxes, which are steadily going up everywhere. They affect the farmers who still managed to retain some of their assets, but who might soon lose them, because today from every quarter people seem to pile taxes upon taxes on their neighbours' property.
We heard this afternoon the speech of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), the former minister of agriculture. I have here a copy of Le Droit dated November 12, 1962. At that period, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle headed the Department of Agriculture. He was quoted as saying:
The Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Hamilton, stated recently that the milk surplus is getting so large in Canada that strong and positive action will have to be taken to ease the situation.
The minister said that no government wants to force producers to reduce their production, but it is up to the federal government to warn the producers when they should reduce production voluntary or face a cut in support prices.
In other words, the minister of agriculture asked the Canadian farmers to reduce production if they want to enjoy the benefit of support prices for the products concerned. And

I have other recent press clippings concerning the administration of the new Minister of Agriculture. In Le Droit of July 31, 1963, one could read the following headline:
Skimmed milk surplus thrown away.
And again in Le Droit of September 13, 1963:
Our wheat surplus to be sold even at a lost.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I quoted those headlines to point out to the house that the problem facing agriculture today is not one of production but one of distribution. Milk, butter and cheese are needed in every part of the country. Canadians have a great need of a better and more diversified agricultural production.
I have here a press clipping dated September 14, 1963, where it is mentioned that a scheme has been set up in the United States providing stamps for the disposal of agricultural surplus. That scheme is called:
IText]
The food stamp plan-chiefly sponsored by congresswoman Leonor K. Sullivan (Democrat, Montana) and Senator Hubert H. Humphrey (Democrat, Minnesota)-is proving a success, according to the New York Times. A report it carried sharply refuted past predictions that the program would prove a failure.
"A new 'currency' is finding its way into the cash registers of supermarkets and corner groceries," the Times said-
Under the program, a family certified by a local welfare agency can exchange the amount of money it normally would spend on food for coupons of greater value-
In the year ended last June 30, the Times reported, $31.2 million of food at retail prices was purchased by food stamps. Of this total, $18.6 million was paid by the government. Thus, needy families got $1 worth of food for 40 cents.

Mr. Speaker, that plan was applied in the United States. At the beginning, it was criticised and people predicted that it would be a failure. Nowadays, it is realized that the plan was a real success. It enabled the United States to dispose of a part of the farm production and I think it would be a good thing for our government, which so often follows the pattern set by the United States, to get the details of that plan in order to apply it here.
Our farm production is still plentiful nowadays. We have people who are in need, and if the government would set up a system of coupons to enable needy families to exchange them for the sums of money they spend each week to purchase food, a family spending $30 each week on food could obtain $45 worth of coupons. That would mean an increase in food expenditures and an increase in the disposal of our stocks. Then we could sell our products on our domestic markets before
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking sending them abroad so that foreign countries might benefit from our abundant production.
Mr. Speaker, I wish that the Minister of Agriculture would be allowed to apply that coupon system. It would certainly help our families with an inadequate income and our farmers would be quite satisfied to sell their production at home.
Mr. Speaker, I call your attention to these suggestions and I wish the Minister of Agriculture would adopt them so that, in a year from now, the farming situation might be changed in Canada and so that the Liberal party would not be in the same position as the Conservative party which was rejected by the people before they could apply their beautiful policies.
I hope that the Minister of Agriculture can put those suggestions into practice as soon as possible, so that our people can benefit from a more adequate farm policy.

X was somewhat surprised at the wording of the motion which accuses the government of failing to take effective action with regard to eastern agriculture and, in particular, with respect to feed grain for eastern Canada. I should like to recall a comment made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he was minister of agriculture. In 1962, he stated in a speech in western Canada that, now the problems of western Canada were resolved, he intended to turn his attention to eastern Canada. Well, if the

minister had paid any attention to eastern Canada prior to the election of June, 1962, he would not have been obliged to turn his attention in that direction during the campaign.
It has been suggested that we should have made much more progress with the legislation we have brought before the house. I venture to say that if this government is guilty of any misdemeanor whatsoever, it is that we have tried too hard. The twenty fourth parliament was dissolved on April 19, 1962. The date of the general election was June 18 of the same year and the writs were all returned by July 18. The twenty fifth parliament met on September 27, and from July 18 to September 27 there are 71 days. This, under the former administration, was called a cooling off period. In the twenty sixth parliament the election was held on April 8, 1963; the writs were returned on May 8 and parliament met on May 16, eight days after the writs had been returned. Now, with 67 legislative days having gone by, we have presented much more legislation than was presented, probably, during a much longer period under the previous administration, during the time when we were told to cool off.
The government has been criticized for not taking effective action with regard to eastern agriculture, and particular attention has been drawn to the desirability. of having a stable price for supplies of Canadian feed grain, and an opportunity for the expansion of eastern feed grain production. I have already indicated that a feed grain policy was announced on August 22. Implementation of this policy will mean that ample supplies of feed grain are to be placed in terminals in eastern Canada before the closing of navigation, and that assistance would be given to the movement of this grain to eastern terminals. In addition, the government proposes to introduce a forward pricing policy which would take much of the risk out of the movement of grain. Thus, the present government has moved much further along these lines than did the previous administration, which was content to follow the policies which were in force since 1941.
I should like to review some of the problems of eastern agriculture-problems, I may say, of which the present government is fully cognizant. Most of us realize that after the last war there was a tremendous increase in mechanization in the industry. Many farms in Canada were not able to use machinery as it became available, but many others found themselves able to use this equipment and were thus placed at a tremendous production advantage. Those which were not were placed at a corresponding disadvantage. I have been in the county of Bellechasse in Quebec and

I have been in New Brunswick. I believe farmers in such areas as these are at a tremendous disadvantage. When we think of agriculture as a whole, we realize that we are being our own worst enemies, because by the use of machinery we have increased our efficiency to a point where 25 per cent fewer farmers have produced 50 per cent more products. We have reached a situation where production per man hour has increased by 70 per cent. In fact, we have increased our efficiency to the point where we are producing more than we can conveniently sell at satisfactory prices. This is the penalty of over-efficiency. The result, of course, in the government's view is that eastern agriculture has to have some special attention. These many areas that I have mentioned have to be taken into consideration. We have to find new land uses for many of these areas, and some real assistance is going to have to be provided whether under the ARDA program or by some other means.
We believe that probably one of the real causes of the problem in eastern Canada was the tremendous increase in the cost of production at a time when farmers' income remained relatively constant. Our incomes have remained fairly constant since 1945, while our production expenses have increased by approximately 50 per cent. Therefore it does not require much of a businessman to realize that the eastern farmer as a result of this phenomenon is going to be placed at a tremendous disadvantage.
I also want to suggest that probably one of the main reasons we were placed at this great disadvantage lies in the fact that the economic growth of the country had slowed down. We had unemployment and therefore we had to discontinue much of our immigration. As a matter of fact, in 1962 more people left Canada than came to Canada. This is an unfortunate situation.
I suggest to the house that probably what Canada needs more than anything else is a buoyant industrial community and business community which will integrate and employ more people in Canada. There is nothing that the farmer needs more than another 10,000,000 mouths to feed, which would enable us to have more of our markets close to home and make us less dependant on export trade. So, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the criticism that has been levelled against the government is quite unjustified and unfounded. I also suggest that the policies that have been put into effect in the comparatively short time that this government has been in power are worthy of the confidence and support of the entire house.
Eastern Agricultural Policy Lacking

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that all members of the house, whether they represent farming communities and farmers directly or indirectly, are truly interested in the welfare of the Canadian farmer, and truly believe that something must be done to help their lot in the industrial country that we have today. That is why I believe it is unfortunate indeed that we who have waited so long to hear some indication of an agricultural policy from the government had to take the step of moving an amendment to a supply motion in order, by debate, to prod the government, we hoped, into an announcement of a definite agricultural policy.
We were very pleased indeed to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) rise in his place this afternoon. We thought that at last we would hear what the government proposed in the way of an agricultural policy to carry this country forward. May I say that I think nearly every member on this side of the house was shocked by the speech we heard from him this afternoon. We were literally shocked to hear a minister of the crown refer to a policy outlined by a former minister, in his sincere desire to appraise and put before the government the problems of agriculture, as a bunch of junk. I believe those were the minister's words.
This seems to me a very ill advised remark to be made by the man who is the head of the Department of Agriculture. We have watched this man since he took office. I have a great deal of admiration for him. We have watched his dynamic personality. We have watched the way that he proposes to meet all problems head on. But when he got up this afternoon and gave that very weak and miserable outline of policy we were, as I said before, shocked. But when you analyse the policy and analyse the man you can understand why he would make such a speech this afternoon. This man is a businessman. This man is a salesman. This man can sell; but when he has nothing to sell the result is exactly what we heard today.
We hoped to hear some enunciation of policy by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Beer). I think the hon. member for Peel is sincere in his position and in his desire to help agriculture, but once again we heard no explanation of policy. We heard a political speech such as we might hear on the hustings. It is unfortunate indeed that government speakers would resort to political tirades at a time like this, when farmers all over the country are waiting for some indication of a policy.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that in July when the hon. member for Peel, substituting for the minister, was invited

by the millers and elevator men of southwestern Ontario to speak to them he did develop his theme with a great deal of painstaking effort. But, Mr. Speaker, his theme was not the grain policy of the country. Rather, it was the official opening on the first day of parliament. When these same gentlemen asked the hon. member for Peel what the policy of the government was on grain, he said it had not been formulated yet and when it was formulated it would be announced to the house and to the people.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
